The Decimated Wavelet Transform (DWT) is a widely used technique in signal and image processing for analyzing and decomposing signals into different frequency components. The DWT has various applications, including signal denoising, compression, feature extraction, image processing, and time series analysis. While the DWT involves downsampling the signal at each level of decomposition, the SWT avoids this downsampling, resulting in a **shift-invariant** wavelet transform that preserves **the original signal length** throughout the analysis. The Undecimated Wavelet Transform is commonly used in various applications, including signal and image denoising, feature extraction, time-frequency analysis, and biomedical signal processing. results.title: Wavelets in Image Processing: A Guide for Beginners
results.content: # How can you use wavelets in image processing? One of the techniques that can be used for image processing is wavelet transform, which is a mathematical tool that decomposes an image into different frequency components. Wavelet transform can be useful for various applications, such as compression, denoising, edge detection, and feature extraction. In this article, you will learn how to use wavelets in image processing and what are some of the benefits and challenges of this method. Wavelets are powerful in image processing for tasks like compression, denoising, and feature extraction. Wavelet transforms break down an image into approximation and detail coefficients, allowing selective manipulation of details. This enables superior compression ratios, noise reduction, and feature preservation compared to traditional methods, making wavelets a versatile tool for enhancing various aspects of image analysis and processing. Wavelets are used in image processing for various purposes: 1- Compression: Wavelets enable effective reduction of image file sizes while maintaining quality. 3- Feature Extraction: Wavelets isolate specific image features like edges, aiding in pattern recognition and detailed analysis. - On the other hand, Wavelets offer both spatial and frequency localization and capture localized features and details within an image. Wavelets can be used for compression by applying DWT to an image and obtaining a set of coefficients that represent the image at different resolutions. Wavelets can be used for denoising by applying DWT to an image and obtaining a set of coefficients that represent the image at different frequencies. The advantage of wavelet denoising is that it can adapt to the local features of the image and preserve the edges and textures. Wavelets can be used for edge detection by applying DWT to an image and obtaining a set of coefficients that represent the image at different orientations and scales. The advantage of wavelet edge detection is that it can capture the multiscale and multidirectional features of the image and avoid noise and aliasing effects. Wavelets can be used for feature extraction by applying DWT to an image and obtaining a set of coefficients that represent the image at different levels of detail and complexity. Using wavelet decomposition for feature extraction goes beyond capturing the characteristics of the image.

results.title: Lifting scheme - Wikipedia
results.content: The **lifting scheme** is a technique for both designing wavelets and performing the discrete wavelet transform (DWT). In an implementation, it is often worthwhile to merge these steps and design the wavelet filters *while* performing the wavelet transform. The lifting scheme factorizes any discrete wavelet transform with finite filters into a series of elementary convolution operators, so-called lifting steps, which reduces the number of arithmetic operations by nearly a factor two. The simplest version of a forward wavelet transform expressed in the lifting scheme is shown in the figure above. The predict step calculates the wavelet function in the wavelet transform. As mentioned above, the lifting scheme is an alternative technique for performing the DWT using biorthogonal wavelets. In order to perform the DWT using the lifting scheme, the corresponding lifting and scaling steps must be derived from the biorthogonal wavelets. Therefore, every wavelet transform with finite filters can be decomposed into a series of lifting and scaling steps. To perform the CDF 9/7 transform, a total of four lifting steps are required: two predict and two update steps. Every transform by the lifting scheme can be inverted. Every two perfect-reconstruction filter banks can be transformed into each other by a sequence of lifting steps. Although every reconstructable filter bank can be expressed in terms of lifting steps, a general description of the lifting steps is not obvious from a description of a wavelet family. A lifting modifies biorthogonal filters in order to increase the number of vanishing moments of the resulting biorthogonal wavelets, and hopefully their stability and regularity. Each lifting step maintains the filter biorthogonality but provides no control on the Riesz bounds and thus on the stability of the resulting wavelet biorthogonal basis. This is why a lifting procedure also increases the number of vanishing moments of dual wavelets. In the case of classical lifting, this is used in order to "prepare" the signal for the next prediction step. In the generalized lifting scheme the addition/subtraction restriction is avoided by including this step in the mapping. "The Lifting Scheme: A Construction of Second Generation Wavelets" (PDF).
